//: DO NOT hand-edit. Generate this from the web app's appsettings so the storage connection strings have one source of truth: pwsh ./Sync-FunctionSettings.ps1 -Environment Test -AppKind Lyrics
//why-one-file: Same constraint as the C# Function app: the Durable task hub name is resolved by the Functions HOST from %LyricsTaskHubName% in host.json, before any worker configuration exists. A settings file the worker loaded could not supply it.
//in-azure: There are no settings files in Azure. The Function App carries its own Application Settings, and that is the per-environment mechanism.
//second-app: This is the SECOND Function app. The first (MusicSalesApp.Functions) is Windows/.NET and owns FFmpeg for transcoding. This one is Linux/Python because Demucs and the forced aligner are PyTorch, and a Function app is pinned to one language runtime. They share both storage accounts and the same callback secret.

Values.//AzureWebJobsStorage: Functions runtime bookkeeping. Shares the standard account with the task hub.
Values.//StagingStorageConnectionString: STANDARD general-purpose account. Holds the Durable task hub AND the staging container this app writes its derived timings to. Read/write. Premium accounts have no Queue service, which is the whole reason there are two accounts.
Values.//MediaStorageConnectionString: PREMIUM account holding song media. READ ONLY from this app - it reads a song's MP3 and the lyrics the artist pasted, and writes nothing. Stricter than the C# app, which does write cover-art renditions here: those go into a brand-new GUID folder before any row exists, whereas lyrics alignment re-runs against a song whose row already points at its timings.
Values.//LyricsTaskHubName: Referenced as %...% from host.json, so the HOST resolves it before the worker starts - if it is missing the app fails to start. MUST differ between Test and Production: both share one storage account, so a shared hub name would have the two environments stealing each other's orchestrations.
Values.//CallbackBaseUrl: Where results are posted. Must match the environment the containers belong to.
Values.//MediaProcessingApiKey: Must equal the top-level MediaProcessingApiKey in the web app's appsettings for the same environment. Note this authorises THIS app to call the web app; the web app authorises itself to call this one with a function key, which is a separate secret travelling the other way.
Values.//FFMPEG_BINARY: A LINUX ffmpeg. The C# app's bundled ffmpeg.exe is useless here. In Azure this points at the Azure Files mount; the generated local file overrides it to whatever is on PATH, and drops TORCH_HOME/XDG_CACHE_HOME so torch and Demucs use their own caches - those mount paths do not exist on a dev machine.
Values.//TORCH_HOME: Where torchaudio looks for the MMS_FA bundle. Pointed at the mount so the weights are not in the deployment package - they are well over a gigabyte and would not fit.
Values.//XDG_CACHE_HOME: Where Demucs looks for its checkpoints. Same reasoning as TORCH_HOME.
Values.//DEMUCS_SEGMENT: Seconds per chunk. Peak memory scales with this, and an out-of-memory kill is a hard failure - the orchestration deliberately does not retry separation. Raise only with a measurement to back it up.
Values.//threads: Two, matching the cores a 4096 MB Flex instance gets. Left unset, torch spawns as many threads as it thinks it sees and spends the difference on contention.
